Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

who pronoun

who? (a question)

also whom, to whom, with whom, who’s there?

classical

Plaut. Men. 137: Quis homō est?
Catull. 1.1: cui dōnō lepidum novum libellum?

quis, quid

interrogative pronoun: accusative quem, genitive cujus, dative cui, ablative quō; plural quī, quōs, quibus

who?

English “whom” is only the case: quem vīdistī?, whom did you see?; cui?, to whom?; quōcum? (or quīcum?), with whom? Quis homō est? is the stage’s “who’s there?”. Lewis & Short gives quis for the feminine too.

Other words

  • quisnam, quaenam, quidnam — who ever? who, then?

    interrogative pronoun, with nam for emphasis · also used · classical · Hor. S. 2.7.83: quisnam igitur līber? (Lewis & Short)

Examples

  • Quis homō est? — Ego sum.

    Who’s there? — It’s me.Plaut. Men. 137–137b

  • Manē, manē. quis illīc est?

    Wait, wait. Who’s that over there?Plaut. Aul. 655

  • cui dōnō lepidum novum libellum āridā modo pūmice expolītum?

    to whom shall I give my charming new little book, just polished with dry pumice?Catull. 1.1–2

  • quem fugis, āh dēmēns?

    whom are you running from, you madman?Verg. E. 2.60

  • ‘ante’ inquit ‘circumspiciendum est cum quibus edās et bibās quam quid edās et bibās’

    “look first,” he says, “at whom you eat and drink with, then at what you eat and drink”Sen. Ep. 19.10

See also who is it?, whose, which, someone, whoever.
